```{r load}
library(tidyverse)
library(diptest)
library(janitor)
library(flextable)
library(forcats)

# Statistical results and predictor matrices from the analysis scripts.
# Run 01_distances.R, 02_mantel.R and 04_null_diagnostics.R first
# (they write these caches).
d01 <- readRDS("../output/rds/01_distances.rds")
d02 <- readRDS("../output/rds/02_mantel.rds")
d04 <- readRDS("../output/rds/04_diagnostics.rds")

mantel_n6      <- d02$mantel_n6
mantel_n5      <- d02$mantel_n5
supp_partials  <- d02$supp_partials
predictor_mats <- d02$predictor_mats
pretty_pred    <- d02$pretty_pred
md_norm        <- d02$md_norm
pa             <- d02$pa
PAL            <- d02$PAL
make_ft        <- d02$make_ft

coordinates     <- d01$coordinates
time_steps      <- d01$time_steps
group_order     <- d01$group_order

# Null-model diagnostics (04_null_diagnostics.R)
fw_table   <- d04$fw_table
scale_sens <- d04$scale_sens
boot_ci    <- d04$boot_ci
size_check <- d04$size_check

# Figure S4 inputs (precomputed in 01_distances.R; rasters don't survive .rds)
s4_df_ds  <- d01$s4_df_ds
s4_df_nat <- d01$s4_df_nat
s4_zlim   <- d01$s4_zlim
s4_neigh  <- d01$s4_neigh
s4_point  <- d01$s4_point

# Raw attribute data for the descriptive supplementary items.
dataset_blanks <- read.csv("../data/dataset_blanks.csv") %>%
  filter(rowSums(is.na(across(Length:Distal.end))) <= 2)

layer_levels <- c("Pa, 24A", "Ca, Au", "CTC, gic-ars", "CTC, rsa'",
                  "RB, A2", "RB, A1", "RF, A2-A1")

filtered_data <- dataset_blanks %>%
  filter(Blank.type %in% c("Blade", "Bladelet"),
         Preservation == "Complete", Class == "Blank") %>%
  mutate(Layer = gsub("_", ", ", Layer),
         Layer = fct_relevel(Layer, layer_levels))
```

## SM Note 1: Sites overview

### Grotta Paglicci
Grotta Paglicci (Rignano Garganico, Foggia, Apulia; 41.654115N, 15.6149763E, 107 m a.s.l.) is located on the southern slopes of the Gargano promontory, with the plain of Foggia extending to the west. The site is part of a larger karst complex, consisting of a cave and a rock-shelter. It contains one of the most important archaeological sequences in southern Italy, extending from the Lower Paleolithic to the final Epigravettian (Palma di Cesnola, 2004). Excavations were first conducted by F. Zorzi in the 1960s and later resumed in the 1970s by the University of Siena under the direction of A. Palma di Cesnola, followed by A. Ronchitelli. The scientific direction of the site is currently in the hands of FB. The Aurignacian layer 24 was found in the first chamber of the cave, where the stratigraphic sequence is about 12 m thick. This layer is likely covered by the Codola tephra in layer 23C2, which dates to approximately 33,000 cal BP (Giaccio et al., 2008). Layer 24 overlies a stalagmitic crust and a sterile layer; it is about one meter thick and characterized by sandy-silt sediments with very few angular debris. It was further subdivided into seven sub-layers, later subsumed into three horizons: BII-I and A4-0 (Palma di Cesnola, 2004). The lower part of the layer (BII-I) is extremely poor in material culture and will therefore not be used in this study. Radiocarbon dating places BII-I between 41,094–37,249 cal BP (95% probability), while A4–A0 dates to 35,050–32,037 cal BP (95% probability), in agreement with the dating of the overlying Codola tephra. Paglicci is close to chert outcrops (i.e., the Maiolica formation), and toolmakers had access to large-sized, high-quality nodules within a few kilometers of the site. Palma di Cesnola (2004) assigned all sub-layers to the Aurignacian with marginally backed tools (i.e., the Protoaurignacian) based on the presence of retouched bladelets, as also reiterated in Marciani et al. (2020). However, this classification is somewhat at odds with the archaeological data from other Italian sites. This study will thus assess the degree of similarity between the A4–A0 assemblage and the other assemblages.

<br>

### Grotta della Cala
Grotta della Cala (Camerota, Salerno, Campania, 40.00108243N, 015.38095416E, 3 m a.s.l.) is located near the present-day coastline at the base of a hilly-mountainous landscape. The cave opens in dolomitic limestone and contains a long stratigraphic sequence spanning the Middle Paleolithic to the Bronze Age (Moroni et al., 2016). Excavations began in 1966 under the direction of A. Palma di Cesnola and later P. Gambassini. Renewed excavations are directed by AM and are currently ongoing. The Aurignacian sequence was found above an Uluzzian layer (UL14) near the cave entrance (Benini et al., 1997). The Aurignacian deposit (~40 cm thick) was rather homogeneous but further divided into four sub-layers (AU13–AU10) based on natural lithostratigraphic differences. The sequence is sealed by a strongly cemented layer (AU10), creating a clear boundary with the subsequent Early Gravettian layer (Martini et al., 2018). New dating shows that the Aurignacian sequence dates to after 40,000 years ago, with the Uluzzian-Aurignacian boundary at 40,097–37,761 cal BP (68.3% probability) (Higham et al., 2024). The main raw materials used at La Cala are chert and radiolarite with different knapping qualities. In several cases, raw materials were collected as small pebbles within 0–15 km of the site (Benini et al., 1997; Martini et al., 2003). A few tools and cores were made on exogenous chert, likely originating from an area approximately 200 km from the site (Falcucci et al., 2025b). All Aurignacian sub-layers are techno-typologically homogeneous and can be assigned to the EA based on the intensive use of carinated technology and the presence of two split-based antler points (Falcucci et al., 2025b). We thus merge all sub-layers into a single assemblage for our comparative analysis (i.e., Ca_Au).

<br>

### Grotta di Castelcivita
Grotta di Castelcivita (Castelcivita, Salerno, Campania; 40.49563600N, 015.20922177E, 94 m a.s.l.) is located at the base of the Alburni massif, part of the southern Italian Apennines. The cave is part of an extensive karst system, with excavations near the cave entrance (Gambassini, 1997). The excavations revealed a thick stratigraphic sequence, which was interrupted around 40,000 years ago by the Campanian Ignimbrite super-eruption from the Phlegraean Fields (Giaccio et al., 2017). Excavations began under P. Gambassini in 1975 and were later conducted by A. Ronchitelli. They continue today under the direction of AM. The Aurignacian sequence rsa’–ars was found directly above the Uluzzian layer rsa’’ (Gambassini, 1997). Layers were divided based on sedimentological differences: rsa’ (~12–25 cm thick) is a fine-grained reddish sediments dominated by silt and sand, with scattered small limestone debris (2–4 cm). Layer gic (~20 cm thick) is extensively concreted and yellowish; layer ars is sandy but lighter (i.e., orange) than rsa’. The sealing of the sequence by the Campanian Ignimbrite provides a clear chronological limit for the Aurignacian at the site. New dating allows modeling the start of rsa’ at 41,935 – 40,756 (at 95% probability) (Higham et al., 2024). Fine-grained chert is the most common raw material across the rsa’–ars assemblages, procured as blocks in the vicinity of the cave or as river pebbles (Falcucci et al., 2024a; Gambassini, 1997). Block size and quality vary, and fragments suitable for knapping were preferentially brought to the site, reducing the production of larger blanks such as blades (Falcucci et al., 2024a). Techno-typological studies reveal a shift from the PA in layer rsa’ to the EA in layers gic and ars. EA layers contain miniaturized retouched bladelets produced from carinated cores, which give the assemblage a marked regional signature. In this study, gic and ars are analyzed as single assemblages due to their chronological closeness and technological similarity.

<br>

### Riparo Bombrini
Riparo Bombrini (Ventimiglia, Imperia, Liguria; 43.46596N, 07.3276E, ca. 16 m a.s.l.) is part of the Balzi Rossi complex, a limestone cliff with rich archaeological deposits near the Tyrrhenian Sea, in the Liguro-Provençal Arc (Ryan et al., 2024). The rockshelter may have been the eastern end of a talus extending from Grotta del Caviglione (Negrino & Riel-Salvatore, 2018; Riel-Salvatore & Negrino, 2018a, 2018b). Scientific exploration began in 1938, but systematic excavations started in 1976 under G. Vicino, followed by B. Holt and FN (2002–2005) (Holt et al., 2019), and FN and JRS (2015–2022) (Riel-Salvatore et al., 2023). The Aurignacian deposit (layers A2–A0) overlies a semi-sterile Mousterian layer (Riel-Salvatore et al., 2022). Layers A2 and A1 consist of yellowish clayey loam with abundant angular clasts and large blocks detached from the vault. A small pocket of sediment above A1 is designated A0. Radiocarbon dating places A2 at 41,200-39,100 cal BP (95% probability) encompassing Heinrich Event 4, while A1 was deposited between 38,524 and 34,337 cal BP (95% probability), mostly during Greenland Interstadial 8 (Benazzi et al., 2015; Negrino & Riel-Salvatore, 2018). Local cherts (within ~5 km) were mainly used for flake production due to their poor quality, while laminar productions often relied on exogenous raw materials (chert and radiolarite) sourced across a wide area, from the Rhône Valley to the Marche region (Falcucci et al., 2025a; Riel-Salvatore & Negrino, 2018b). Both A2 and A1 are assigned to the Protoaurignacian, reflecting different mobility strategies: primarily logistical for A2 and residential for A1 (Falcucci et al., 2025a; Riel-Salvatore & Negrino, 2018b). These layers will be analyzed as single units, while the very small EA assemblage in A0 is excluded from the comparative analysis.

<br>

### Grotta di Fumane
Grotta di Fumane (Fumane, Verona, Veneto; 45.5918287N, 10.9051824E, 350 m a.s.l.) is located in the western Monti Lessini Plateau within the Venetian pre-Alps (Bartolomei et al., 1992). The cave is part of a karst complex, with deposits found in the upper section featuring a main cavity and two associated tunnels (Peresani, 2022). Excavations revealed a deep stratigraphic sequence spanning from MIS4 to Heinrich Event 3, when the cave ceiling collapsed. Scientific exploration began in 1964, with systematic excavations from 1988 under A. Broglio and M. Cremaschi and then MP. The Aurignacian sequence directly overlies the Uluzzian (stratigraphic unit A3) and is found in both fine-grained, thin horizontally bedded stratigraphic units (A2 and A1) and the overlying macro-unit D. The transition to macro-unit D is marked by a sharp lithological shift and evidence of multiple landslides, likely due to climatic deterioration (Kehl et al., 2025; López-García et al., 2015). Stratigraphic units A2 and A1 date to 42,000–39,250 cal BP (95.4% probability), while the upper Aurignacian in macro-unit D3 accumulated during Heinrich Event 4 (Higham et al., 2009; Marín-Arroyo et al., 2023). High-quality chert nodules form the western Monti Lessini Plateau were available within 5–15 km, found both in primary and secondary outcrops (Bertola, 2001; Bertola et al., 2018). Stratigraphic units A2 and A1 were analyzed by several researchers and assigned to the Protoaurignacian (Bertola et al., 2013; De Stefani, 2003; Falcucci et al., 2017; Falcucci et al., 2020). Recent lithic taphonomic studies prompted Falcucci et al. (2024b) to treat A2–A1 as a single stratigraphic unit and assign D3b alpha to the Early Aurignacian. Due to the limited sample size, D3b alpha is excluded from comparative analysis.

## Tables

### Table S1

```{r table-s1}
filtered_data %>%
  group_by(Layer) %>%
  summarise(dip_p = round(dip.test(Width)$p.value, 2),
            n = n(), .groups = "drop") %>%
  flextable() %>% theme_vanilla() %>% autofit()
```

**Table S1.** Hartigan's dip test for unimodality of blade and bladelet widths per assemblage. Non-significant *p*-values (> 0.05) are consistent with a unimodal width distribution.

<br>

### Table S2

```{r table-s2}
mantel_n6 |>
  transmute(predictor, r6 = r_pearson, p6 = p_pearson) |>
  left_join(transmute(mantel_n5, predictor, r5 = r_pearson, p5 = p_pearson),
            by = "predictor") |>
  mutate(shift = r5 - r6) |>
  arrange(desc(r6)) |>
  transmute(Predictor = pretty_pred[predictor],
            `r (n=6)` = sprintf("%.3f", r6), `p (n=6)` = sprintf("%.3f", p6),
            `r (n=5)` = sprintf("%.3f", r5), `p (n=5)` = sprintf("%.3f", p5),
            `delta r` = sprintf("%+.3f", shift)) |>
  make_ft()
```

**Table S2.** Pearson Mantel correlations between combined lithic distance and each candidate predictor, for the full dataset (n = 6) and with Paglicci 24A excluded (n = 5). Δr is the change in r (n = 5 minus n = 6). Spearman equivalents are reported in the main text. *p*-values are marginal and uncorrected for the seven-predictor screen; family-wise values are given in Table S4.

<br>

### Table S3

```{r table-s3}
supp_partials |>
  transmute(Control = control, Predictor = predictor,
            `r (partial)` = sprintf("%.3f", r_partial),
            `p` = sprintf("%.3f", p_partial)) |>
  make_ft() |> flextable::bold(part = "header")
```

**Table S3.** Partial Mantel correlations (Spearman) between combined lithic distance and each predictor, each controlled for one of the three focal predictors (Costpath, Chronology, or native TAP), at n = 5 (Paglicci excluded). *p*-values are uncorrected.

<br>

### Table S4

```{r table-s4}
fw_table |>
  transmute(Predictor,
            `r (n=6)` = sprintf("%.3f", r_n6),
            `p marginal (n=6)` = sprintf("%.3f", p_marginal),
            `r (n=5)` = sprintf("%.3f", r_n5),
            `p marginal (n=5)` = sprintf("%.3f", p_marginal5)) |>
  make_ft()
```

**Table S4.** Exact permutation probabilities for each candidate predictor, for the full dataset (n = 6) and with Paglicci 24A excluded (n = 5). The values above are marginal, that is, uncorrected for the fact that seven predictors were screened. Correcting for the screen, by recomputing all seven correlations under every relabelling and retaining the largest, gives a family-wise probability of `r sprintf("%.3f", d04$fw6$p_familywise)` for the full dataset (largest r = `r sprintf("%.3f", d04$fw6$obs_max)`) and `r sprintf("%.3f", d04$fw5$p_familywise)` for the five-assemblage subset (largest r = `r sprintf("%.3f", d04$fw5$obs_max)`). Neither is below the conventional 0.05 threshold.

<br>

### Table S5

```{r table-s6}
size_check |>
  transmute(Assemblage = assemblage,
            `Blanks (n)` = n_blanks, `Cores (n)` = n_cores,
            `Mean blank distance` = sprintf("%.3f", mean_blank),
            `Mean core distance`  = sprintf("%.3f", mean_core),
            `Mean combined distance` = sprintf("%.3f", mean_comb)) |>
  make_ft()
```

**Table S5.** Assemblage sample size and technological isolation. Sample sizes for blanks and cores in each assemblage compared with mean technological distance to the other assemblages in the combined FLEXDIST matrix. The table evaluates whether apparent technological isolation could be inflated by small sample size. No such relationship is observed: assemblage size does not predict mean technological distance, and the smallest core sample, Riparo Bombrini A2, is among the least isolated assemblages.

## Figures

### Figure S1

```{r figure-s1, fig.width=9, fig.height=7}
filtered_data %>%
  count(Layer, Blank.type) %>%
  group_by(Layer) %>% mutate(prop = n / sum(n)) %>% ungroup() %>%
  ggplot(aes(Layer, prop, fill = Blank.type)) +
  geom_col(colour = "grey25", linewidth = 0.3) +
  geom_text(aes(label = scales::percent(prop, accuracy = 1)),
            position = position_stack(vjust = 0.5), size = 3) +
  scale_fill_brewer(palette = "Set2", name = "Blank") +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::percent) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Relative frequency") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 13) +
  theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 45, hjust = 1),
        legend.position = "bottom")
```

**Figure S1.** Relative frequency of blank types (blades vs bladelets) across the studied assemblages.

<br>

### Figure S2

```{r figure-s2, fig.width=9, fig.height=8}
area_data <- filtered_data %>%
  mutate(
    # merge the two highest cortex classes into a single 66-100% bin
    CortexMerged = case_when(Cortex %in% c("66-99%", "100%") ~ "66-100%",
                             TRUE ~ Cortex),
    CortexMerged = factor(CortexMerged,
                          levels = c("0%", "1-33%", "33-66%", "66-100%")),
    Area = Length * Width)

area_summary <- area_data %>%
  group_by(Layer, CortexMerged) %>%
  summarise(MeanArea = mean(Area, na.rm = TRUE),
            SE = sd(Area, na.rm = TRUE) / sqrt(n()),
            n = n(), .groups = "drop")

cb_palette <- c("0%" = "#88CCEE", "1-33%" = "#CC6677",
                "33-66%" = "#DDCC77", "66-100%" = "#117733")

ggplot(area_summary, aes(CortexMerged, MeanArea, fill = CortexMerged)) +
  geom_col(colour = "black", linewidth = 0.4) +
  geom_errorbar(aes(ymin = MeanArea - SE, ymax = MeanArea + SE),
                width = 0.25, linewidth = 0.6) +
  facet_wrap(~ Layer, ncol = 2) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = cb_palette) +
  scale_y_continuous(expand = expansion(mult = c(0, 0.1))) +
  labs(x = "Cortex coverage",
       y = expression(bold("Mean blank area (mm"^2*")")), fill = "Cortex") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 13) +
  theme(panel.grid.major.x = element_blank(),
        panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
        panel.border = element_rect(colour = "gray70", fill = NA),
        strip.background = element_rect(fill = "gray90", colour = NA),
        strip.text = element_text(face = "bold"),
        axis.title = element_text(face = "bold"),
        axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 35, hjust = 1),
        legend.position = "bottom")
```

**Figure S2.** Blank size (Length × Width, mm²) of complete blades and bladelets in each assemblage, grouped by cortical coverage class (0%, 1–33%, 33–66%, 66–100%; the original 66–99% and 100% classes are merged). Bars show the mean per class within each assemblage; error bars are ± 1 standard error.

### Figure S3

```{r figure-s3, fig.width=10, fig.height=7}
mat_to_pairs <- function(mat, value_name) {
  lt  <- which(lower.tri(mat), arr.ind = TRUE)
  out <- data.frame(site1 = rownames(mat)[lt[, 1]],
                    site2 = rownames(mat)[lt[, 2]],
                    val = mat[lt], stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
  out$pair <- paste0(pmin(out$site1, out$site2), "_", pmax(out$site1, out$site2))
  out$involves_paglicci <- out$site1 == pa | out$site2 == pa
  names(out)[names(out) == "val"] <- value_name
  out[, c("pair", value_name, "involves_paglicci")]
}
predictors_to_plot <- c("TAP", "TAP_ds", "MAT", "MAT_ds", "chrono", "costpath")

pred_long <- do.call(rbind, lapply(predictors_to_plot, function(p) {
  df <- mat_to_pairs(predictor_mats[[p]], "predictor_value"); df$predictor <- p
  df[, c("pair", "predictor", "predictor_value")]
}))
resp_long <- mat_to_pairs(md_norm, "lithic")
all_pairs <- pred_long |>
  left_join(resp_long[, c("pair", "lithic", "involves_paglicci")], by = "pair")
all_pairs$predictor <- factor(all_pairs$predictor, levels = predictors_to_plot)

mantel_grid <- mantel_n6 |>
  filter(predictor %in% predictors_to_plot) |>
  transmute(predictor = factor(predictor, levels = predictors_to_plot),
            label = sprintf("r = %.2f, p = %.3f", r_spearman, p_spearman))

ggplot(all_pairs, aes(predictor_value, lithic)) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = TRUE, colour = PAL$grey_dark,
              fill = "grey88", alpha = 0.4, linewidth = 0.6) +
  geom_point(aes(colour = involves_paglicci), size = 2.6, alpha = 0.85) +
  geom_text(data = mantel_grid, aes(x = -Inf, y = Inf, label = label),
            hjust = -0.08, vjust = 1.4, size = 3.3, colour = "grey30",
            inherit.aes = FALSE) +
  facet_wrap(~ predictor, scales = "free_x", ncol = 3,
             labeller = labeller(predictor = pretty_pred)) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c("FALSE" = PAL$grey_dark, "TRUE" = PAL$red),
                      labels = c("Other pairs", "Includes Paglicci"), name = NULL) +
  labs(x = "Predictor distance", y = "Combined lithic distance") +
  theme_bw(base_size = 11) +
  theme(strip.background = element_rect(fill = "grey92", colour = NA),
        strip.text = element_text(face = "bold"),
        legend.position = "bottom", panel.grid.minor = element_blank())
```

**Figure S3.** Combined lithic distance against each candidate predictor (15 pairwise comparisons); pairs involving Paglicci 24A are highlighted. Lines show the linear trend with 95% confidence bands; Spearman Mantel r and p are annotated per panel.

### Figure S4

```{r figure-s4, fig.width=10, fig.height=5}
# TAP around Paglicci, downscaled vs native. All inputs were precomputed in
# 01_distances.R (terra rasters do not survive .rds serialization).
library(patchwork)

tap_panel <- function(df, title) {
  ggplot(df, aes(x, y, fill = TAP)) +
    geom_raster() +
    geom_point(data = s4_point, aes(x, y), inherit.aes = FALSE,
               shape = 21, fill = "red", colour = "white", size = 3) +
    geom_text(data = s4_point, aes(x, y, label = "Pa 24A"), inherit.aes = FALSE,
              colour = "red", fontface = "bold", hjust = -0.15, size = 3.3) +
    scale_fill_viridis_c(option = "mako", direction = -1, limits = s4_zlim,
                         name = "TAP (mm)") +
    coord_equal() + labs(title = title, x = NULL, y = NULL) +
    theme_minimal(base_size = 11) +
    theme(plot.title = element_text(face = "bold", hjust = 0.5))
}

(tap_panel(s4_df_ds,  "TAP downscaled (10 arc-min) - 34 ka") |
 tap_panel(s4_df_nat, "TAP native (30 arc-min) - 34 ka")) +
  plot_layout(guides = "collect") & theme(legend.position = "right")
```

```{r figure-s4-check}
print(s4_neigh)
cat(sprintf("\nPaglicci cell:  downscaled = %d mm,  native = %d mm\n",
            s4_neigh$downscaled[1], s4_neigh$native[1]))
cat(sprintf("Neighbour mean: downscaled = %d mm,  native = %d mm\n",
            round(mean(s4_neigh$downscaled[-1])),
            round(mean(s4_neigh$native[-1]))))
```

**Figure S4.** Total annual precipitation around Paglicci 24A at 34 ka, downscaled (left) versus native (right), on a shared colour scale. The accompanying table compares the value at Paglicci's grid cell with its eight neighbours in each reconstruction, showing that the low downscaled value is shared across the neighbourhood rather than confined to a single cell: the dry signal is a coherent feature of the reconstructed surface over the Tavoliere and the Gargano rain shadow, not a grid-cell artefact.

### Figure S5

```{r figure-s5, fig.width=7, fig.height=5}
boot_ci |>
  ggplot(aes(x = reorder(Predictor, observed))) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, colour = "grey75") +
  geom_linerange(aes(ymin = lwr, ymax = upr), linewidth = 0.8,
                 colour = PAL$grey_dark) +
  geom_point(aes(y = observed), size = 3.4, colour = PAL$red) +
  coord_flip() +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Mantel r (Spearman), bootstrap 95% CI") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 11) +
  theme(panel.grid.minor = element_blank())
```

**Figure S5.** Bootstrap 95% confidence intervals on the Mantel coefficients, from 2,000 specimen-level resamples within assemblage propagated through the group centroids and the combined distance matrix (PC loadings held fixed). Red points are the observed coefficients. The intervals of the leading predictors overlap substantially, so their ranking is not determined by the data.

## SM Note 2: Bayesian models

### Grotta Paglicci

``` 
Plot()
{
Resolution=100;
Curve("IntCal20","IntCal20.14c");
Outlier_Model("General",T(5),U(0,4),"t");
Sequence("Paglicci Aurignacian")
  {
    Boundary("Start Aurignacian");
    Phase("Aurignacian 24B1-2")
     {
    R_Date("24B1-2", 34300, 800)
         {
          Outlier("General", 0.05);
         };
     Date("Aurignacian 24B1-2");
        };
``` 
